785.title: Visit the graves
785.hook: the Prophet encouraged visiting graves, for they remind of death and the hereafter (Sahih Muslim)
785.howItsDone: Muslims visit graves, in some communities on Fridays or around the Eids, greeting the dead with a salam, reciting Quran and praying for mercy for them; practices such as praying to the dead or wailing at graves are discouraged.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Ibrahim, the Prophet's little son, and tears the Prophet called mercy. Your line was this is mercy. Today, the same Prophet stands at a grave.

A grave, and a grown man standing at it, crying. It's his mother's grave, and he has come to see where she lies. The people with him start crying too, because he is. The man is the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and the scene is in Sahih Muslim, a collection of reports of his words and deeds. When he speaks, he ends with advice for everyone standing there, and for anyone who has ever avoided a cemetery.
screen: `A MAN AT HIS MOTHER'S GRAVE.` → `EVERYONE AROUND HIM WEEPS.` → `THEN HE SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: In another report in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says something surprising: I had forbidden you to visit graves, but now visit them. A rule was set, then lifted, and the report keeps both halves, the old no and the new yes, in a single sentence. At his mother's grave, he gives the reason plainly: visit the graves, for they remind you of death. Reports in other collections add that they remind you of the hereafter. The point isn't to stay sad. A grave is a teacher. It doesn't lecture. It just stands there with a name on it, saying: this happens to everyone, and then comes what comes next. The hadith don't picture walking into a cemetery in silence. Reports in the same collection describe a greeting to the people in the graves: peace be upon you, dwellers of these homes, believers; and we, God willing, will join you. The dead are spoken to as neighbors. It's easy to arrange a life that never passes a grave; in some towns, cemeteries sit at the edge, behind walls. This hadith turns that around: go on purpose, so the living remember they are on the same road. In Muslim teaching, the visit is a kindness to the dead, with prayers for them, and to the living, a reminder while there's still time to use it.
screen: `FORBIDDEN, THEN ENCOURAGED.` · `GRAVES REMIND YOU OF DEATH.` · `GREET THE DEAD AS NEIGHBORS.` · `GO ON PURPOSE.` · then, large: `THEY REMIND US.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a grave you know, a grandparent's, a friend's, a stranger's you once walked past, or a place where someone's ashes rest, and stand there in your mind, seeing the ground, the stone, the name. Let it remind you of what it reminds you of, without pushing. If you pray, you can greet the dead there, or ask mercy for them, in words you already know.
Sahih Muslim, the hadith collection where the Prophet, having once forbidden it, now tells people to visit graves, because they remind the living of death. Today's word.
Your line: they remind us. A grave teaches without saying a word. Day seven hundred eighty-five, done.

786.title: Going home
786.hook: at Sikh funerals the bedtime prayer Kirtan Sohila is sung, and death is spoken of as going home (Guru Granth Sahib 12–13)
786.howItsDone: Sikhs recite Kirtan Sohila before sleep each night, and at a cremation it is recited after the pyre is lit, followed by the Ardas; mourners are asked to sing hymns rather than wail.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Sahih Muslim, where the Prophet says to visit graves. Your line was they remind us. Today, Sikh hymns sung at bedtime, and at the very end.

Night, in a Sikh home. The lights are low, the day's noise is over, and before sleep someone reads a short set of hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib. They're called Kirtan Sohila, and they're meant for the end of the day. Now a different scene: a cremation. The family has gathered, the fire has been lit, and the same hymns are sung. The words that close an ordinary evening also close a life. Some readers hear in that a single thought: sleep and death are both a kind of going home.
screen: `A BEDTIME PRAYER.` → `THE SAME HYMNS AT A CREMATION.` → `SLEEP AND DEATH, BOTH HOMEWARD.`

segments.voice: The Sikh code of conduct, the Rehat Maryada, names Kirtan Sohila as the prayer to recite before sleeping. It also says that at a cremation, once the pyre is lit, Kirtan Sohila is recited and the Ardas, the Sikh prayer of petition, is offered. The first hymn, by Guru Nanak, doesn't sound like a funeral at all. It sounds like a wedding. The soul is pictured as a bride whose wedding date has already been written. Her friends are told to gather, to pour oil on the threshold, a wedding custom, and to bless her so she may meet her Lord. In this picture, death isn't a thief at the door. It's the groom's party arriving. The hymn goes on: the call goes out to every home, every day. Remember the One who calls. The day is coming. It's said gently, the way a mother reminds a child that the bus will come in the morning. Sikh teaching speaks of death as the soul returning to the One it came from, and of accepting it as God's will. The Rehat Maryada asks mourners not to wail or beat their breasts, but to turn to the hymns. Grief isn't forbidden; it's given a song. Some readers hear the nightly singing as a small rehearsal for the night that ends everything, and the singing at a cremation as tucking someone in.
screen: `A PRAYER BEFORE SLEEP.` · `THE SOUL AS A BRIDE.` · `THE CALL REACHES EVERY HOME.` · `GRIEF IS GIVEN A SONG.` · then, large: `GOING HOME.`

segments.voice: Hum something quietly, any gentle tune you know well, a lullaby, a hymn, a song from home, low and soft, barely more than breath, and feel it in the chest and the face. Let it be the sound of a day closing, a door shut gently for the night. If you know a line of Sohila, or a prayer of your own tradition, you can hum or say that instead.
Going home: how the Sikh bedtime hymns, Kirtan Sohila, sung each night and at cremations, picture death: a bride's wedding, a call to every home, a soul returning. Today's word.
Your line: tucking someone in. The same song closes a day and a life. Sleep well tonight.

787.title: Knowing how to die
787.hook: Guru Nanak: death wouldn't be called bad if people knew how truly to die
787.howItsDone: Sikhs hear the Gurus' hymns on death in the gurdwara and at funerals, where the evening hymns of Kirtan Sohila are sung; Sikh teaching describes remembering the Name, honest work and service as the way a life prepares for its end.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was going home, how the Sikh bedtime hymns picture death. Your line was tucking someone in.

A family is mourning. Someone says what people say: what a terrible thing, death. And a hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib, the Sikh scripture, answers back, gently. On page 579, in verses Guru Nanak gave for times of mourning, comes a line that, put plainly, runs like this: people, don't call death bad, if only someone knew how truly to die. The hymn doesn't argue that death is pleasant. It moves the problem. The trouble isn't dying. It's not knowing how.
screen: `A FAMILY MOURNS.` → `DON'T CALL DEATH BAD.` → `IF ONE KNEW HOW.`

segments.voice: Death sounds like something that simply happens to you. Nobody takes a class in it. But the hymn speaks of it as a skill, something a person can know or not know. Where is it learned? In Sikh teaching, as the Gurus describe it, a person who lives remembering the divine Name, serving others and living honestly is already practicing for the end. The same verses speak of serving the Lord and of the true court a person goes to after this life. So knowing how to die isn't a last-minute trick. It's what a whole life has been rehearsing. Sikhs have a phrase for this: dying while alive. Some Sikh readers hear it as letting the ego die now, the grasping, the need to win, so that when death comes there's less left to tear away. Readers explain it in different ways, but the shape is simple: practice letting go in small things, and the big letting go is less of a stranger. The hymn was given for mourning. But if a whole life is the rehearsal, then the rehearsal is happening this afternoon, in an hour spent scrolling or an hour spent with someone you love. Read that way, the question shifts from how long a life runs to how the hour in front of you is lived.
screen: `DEATH AS A SKILL.` · `LEARNED BY LIVING.` · `DYING WHILE ALIVE.` · `THE HOUR YOU'RE IN.` · then, large: `KNOWING HOW.`

segments.voice: Look at the next hour of your day, just the next hour: where you'll be, and who will be there. Ask it one quiet question, if this hour were lived well, what would it look like, slower, kinder, one thing done properly instead of three done badly, and let one small picture come. If you pray, you can hold that hour up in your own tradition's words.
Maran, the Gurmukhi word for death in Guru Nanak's hymn, which says the trouble isn't dying, but not knowing how, learned by living. Today's word.
Your line: knowing how. A whole life is the rehearsal. That's day seven hundred eighty-seven.

788.title: The skull's dream
788.hook: Zhuangzi pillows on a skull, which tells him in a dream the dead have no kings and no seasons
788.howItsDone: The Zhuangzi is read in Daoist circles and in Chinese literature classes alike; readers return to its death stories, like the skull, for comfort, for argument and for their humor.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was maran, death, which Guru Nanak said isn't bad for one who knows how to die. Your line was knowing how. Today, a Chinese sage takes a nap on a skull.

A traveler on the road to the state of Chu spots something by the path: a skull, empty, dried out, bleached. The traveler is Zhuangzi, a Daoist thinker whose book often makes serious points through jokes. He pokes the skull with his riding whip and starts asking it questions. Did you love life too greedily? Were you executed? Did you do something shameful and die of the disgrace? Did you starve, or freeze? Or did your years simply run out? Then he pulls the skull over, puts his head on it like a pillow, and goes to sleep.
screen: `A SKULL BY THE ROAD.` → `HOW DID YOU DIE?` → `A PILLOW FOR THE NIGHT.`

segments.voice: In the middle of the night, in chapter eighteen of the Zhuangzi, the skull appears to him in a dream and complains. You talk like a debater, it says. All the things you asked about are troubles of the living. The dead have none of that. Among the dead, it says, there's no ruler above and no servant below, and none of the work of the four seasons. Easy and unhurried, with heaven and earth for its springs and autumns. Even a king on his throne has no happiness greater than this. Zhuangzi doesn't quite believe it. So he makes an offer: what if I asked the one in charge of life to give you back your bones and flesh and skin, and send you home to your parents, your wife and children, your old friends? And the skull frowns deeply. Why would I throw away a king's happiness, it asks, to take up the troubles of the living again? End of story. Some readers take the skull at its word, a picture of death as rest. Others hear Zhuangzi teasing: a skull lecturing a philosopher, in a dream, about a place no one returns from. The book doesn't settle it, and it seems to enjoy not settling it. What it does do is take our fear, poke it with a whip, and use it for a pillow.
screen: `THE SKULL SPEAKS IN A DREAM.` · `NO KINGS, NO SEASONS.` · `WOULD YOU COME BACK?` · `REST, OR A JOKE?` · then, large: `THE SKULL'S DREAM.`

segments.voice: Rest your head on a pillow, a folded arm or the back of a chair, and let its weight really go into it, noticing how much your neck has been holding all day. Then let the skull's question come once, without needing an answer: what am I carrying that I'd be glad to set down?
Zhuangzi, the Daoist thinker who dreamed a skull told him the dead have no kings and no seasons, and wouldn't trade that for life again. Today's word.
Your line: a king's happiness. Whether the skull is joking, the book leaves to you. See you tomorrow.

789.title: First, life
789.hook: asked about death, Confucius: not yet knowing life, how can we know death?
789.howItsDone: The Analects are read and studied by Confucian teachers, students and families; this exchange with Zilu is a passage readers turn to when they ask what Confucius taught about death.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Zhuangzi, whose skull wouldn't trade death for life again. Your line was a king's happiness. Today, a teacher who won't go there at all.

A student asks his teacher the big one. The student is Zilu, one of his disciples. The teacher is Confucius. First Zilu asks how to serve the spirits of the dead. Confucius answers with a question: if you can't yet serve the living, how could you serve the spirits? Zilu doesn't let go. All right, he says. Then may I ask about death? And the answer, in the Analects, comes back short: not yet knowing life, how can you know death?
screen: `ZILU ASKS ABOUT SPIRITS.` → `THEN ABOUT DEATH.` → `NOT YET KNOWING LIFE.`

segments.voice: It can sound like a dodge. A student asks about death and gets a question back. Some readers do hear it that way: a teacher steering away from what he doesn't claim to know. But listen to both answers. Serve the living, then think of serving the spirits. Know life, then ask about death. Neither says the question is foolish. Both say there's an order, and you're not at the end of it yet. That's today's word: first. And Confucius cared about the dead. The Analects speak with care about funerals and about remembering parents after they're gone. One saying in the first book, from his disciple Zengzi, asks for care in the rites when parents die, and for remembering them long after. So the order isn't the living instead of the dead. The way you treat the living is where you learn to honor anyone at all. Zilu wanted the answer to the biggest question. Confucius handed him a smaller, harder job: the life in front of you, the people in front of you, today. If death is a door no one can see through, there's still a whole house on this side of it, and the rooms need tending. Some hear that as wisdom, some as a sidestep. Either way, it sends you back to the kitchen table instead of the stars.
screen: `A DODGE?` · `AN ORDER: FIRST, LIFE.` · `HE CARED FOR THE DEAD.` · `TEND THE HOUSE THIS SIDE.` · then, large: `FIRST, LIFE.`

segments.voice: Notice what's actually around you, the light in the room, a sound outside, the chair holding you up, and bring to mind one living person who's part of your day. What does today ask of you, for them: a call, a meal, a little patience? If death comes to mind, let it, and then gently come back to today.
First: Confucius's order of things. Serve the living before the spirits, know life before death. Today's word.
Your line: the kitchen table. Life first, and the rest in its order. Day seven hundred eighty-nine, done.

790.title: Qingming, sweeping tombs
790.hook: in spring, Chinese families sweep their ancestors' tombs
790.howItsDone: At Qingming, Chinese families travel to their ancestors' graves to clean them, set out food, burn incense and paper offerings, and bow; customs differ by family and region.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was first: Confucius's order, life before death. Your line was the kitchen table. Today, the living go out to care for the dead.

A hillside in spring. Cars parked along the road, families climbing with brooms, buckets, bags of food and bundles of paper. A grandmother points the way. A teenager carries a rake and looks at his phone. At a grave, everyone gets to work: pulling weeds, sweeping the stone, wiping the name clean so it can be read again. Then food set out, incense lit, a bow. Sometimes a picnic right there, the living eating with the dead nearby. This is Qingming, the festival also called tomb-sweeping day.
screen: `A HILLSIDE IN SPRING.` → `BROOMS AND BUCKETS.` → `TOMB-SWEEPING DAY.`

segments.voice: Qingming means clear and bright, and it falls in spring, when the weather is turning and the ground is green again. It's a festival of the season as much as of the dead, which is why, in some places, people also go walking in the countryside or fly kites. The heart of the day is plain physical work. Weeds come out. Dirt is cleared. The stone is washed. Some families add fresh soil to the grave or leave a slip of paper on it to show someone came. Remembering is done with hands. Families set out food and drink the person liked and burn incense, and some burn paper offerings: folded paper money, or paper models of things the dead might need. Customs differ from family to family and region to region, and some families today bring flowers instead. Why do it? Confucian teaching speaks of filial care, the honor owed to parents, and the Analects ask that parents be served with proper rites while alive, buried with proper rites, and remembered with proper rites after. Yesterday Confucius said life first. Here's the other half: when life ends, the care doesn't. It moves to a hillside, with a broom. People who keep Qingming hold its meaning in different ways, some as honoring spirits who are present, some as keeping a family's story alive. Either way, the name on the stone gets read again.
screen: `CLEAR AND BRIGHT.` · `SWEEPING WITH YOUR HANDS.` · `FOOD, INCENSE, PAPER.` · `CARE THAT DOESN'T END.` · then, large: `SWEEP THE TOMB.`

segments.voice: Choose someone who has died, and think of one thing of theirs you have or could reach: a photo frame, a mug, a book, a pair of glasses. If it's near, pick it up and clean it slowly; if not, picture yourself doing it, and let the cleaning be the remembering. If a memory comes with it, let it stay a while.
Qingming: clear and bright, the spring festival when Chinese families sweep their ancestors' tombs, bring food and remember them. Today's word.
Your line: sweep the tomb. Care for the dead can take the shape of a broom. Until tomorrow.

791.title: Día de los Muertos
791.hook: in Mexico families welcome the dead with marigolds, photos and favorite foods
791.howItsDone: For Día de los Muertos, families in Mexico and in Mexican communities elsewhere build ofrendas at home with photos, marigolds, candles and the dead's favorite foods, and families visit and decorate graves; customs vary by region and family.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Qingming, a broom on a spring hillside. Your line was sweep the tomb. Today, the dead come to the family's table.

A small table against the living room wall is filling up. A framed photo of an abuelo in his good hat. Candles. A plate of his favorite food, still warm. A bottle of the soda he liked. Sweet bread. Paper cut into lace in bright colors. And everywhere, orange: marigolds, heaped in pots and scattered in a path of petals toward the door. Nobody is setting this table for the living. It's for the people who have died, and the family expects them. This is the ofrenda, the offering, for Día de los Muertos, the Day of the Dead.
screen: `A TABLE FILLS UP.` → `A PATH OF MARIGOLDS.` → `THE OFRENDA.`

segments.voice: In the way families describe it, the dead return for these days to be with the people who love them. So the ofrenda isn't a memorial in the usual sense. It's hospitality: you put out a guest's favorite food because a guest is coming. The marigolds' color and scent, families say, help guide the dead home, which is why the petals make a path. The photo says who is expected. The water, the food, the candles say welcome, you must be tired from the journey. Families also go to the graves, clean and decorate them with flowers and candles, and stay, sometimes through the night, eating, talking, playing music. It can look like a party. For the families who keep it this way, it is one, a loving one. It comes at the start of November, alongside the Catholic days of All Saints and All Souls, which you met earlier in this block. In Mexico, as the story is often told, those days meet older Indigenous ways of honoring the dead, and families keep it in their own ways. It isn't Halloween. The painted and sugar skulls are smiling, not scary. Look back at the week: graves that remind us, going home, knowing how to die, a skull that wanted to stay dead, life first, a broom on a hillside, and now a table set for guests. Different peoples, different beliefs, and the same quiet refusal to let the dead become strangers.
screen: `THE DEAD COME TO VISIT.` · `MARIGOLDS SHOW THE WAY.` · `A NIGHT AT THE GRAVES.` · `THIS WEEK, LOOKING BACK.` · then, large: `THEY VISIT.`
